subject: Indian Polity
title: Constituent Assembly Formation
content: The Constituent Assembly was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946. It was not directly elected by the people but by members of the Provincial Legislative Assemblies.

subject: Indian Polity
title: First Meeting of the Assembly
content: The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly was held on 9 December 1946. Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha was elected as the temporary/interim President.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Permanent President
content: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly on 11 December 1946.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Drafting Committee
content: The Drafting Committee was formed on 29 August 1947 with Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as its Chairman. It had 7 members in total.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Constitutional Advisor
content: B.N. Rau served as the Constitutional Advisor to the Constituent Assembly and prepared the original draft before the Drafting Committee's work.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Adoption Date
content: The Constitution of India was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949. This day is now celebrated as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas).

subject: Indian Polity
title: Commencement Date
content: The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, a date chosen to commemorate the 1930 declaration of Purna Swaraj. This day is celebrated as Republic Day.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Time Taken to Draft
content: The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months, and 18 days to complete the drafting of the Constitution.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Original Structure
content: The original Constitution had 395 Articles, 22 Parts, and 8 Schedules. It has since been amended many times and now has 12 Schedules.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Borrowed Features
content: India's Constitution borrowed features from various countries: Parliamentary system from the UK, Fundamental Rights from the USA, Directive Principles from Ireland, and federal structure from Canada.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Preamble Overview
content: The Preamble declares India to be a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic, securing Justice, Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity to all citizens.

subject: Indian Polity
title: 42nd Amendment Changes
content: The words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976, along with 'Integrity' after 'Unity'.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Source of Authority
content: The Preamble begins with 'We, the people of India', indicating that the ultimate source of authority for the Constitution is the people of India themselves.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Objectives Resolution
content: The Preamble is based on the 'Objectives Resolution' drafted and moved by Jawaharlal Nehru in the Constituent Assembly on 13 December 1946.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Berubari Case 1960
content: In the Berubari Union case (1960), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution and is therefore not enforceable in a court of law.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Kesavananda Bharati Case 1973
content: In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court reversed its earlier stand and held that the Preamble IS a part of the Constitution, though it can be amended, subject to the 'basic structure' doctrine.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Four Ideals in Preamble
content: The Preamble mentions four ideals: Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (of status and opportunity), and Fraternity (assuring dignity of the individual and unity of the nation).

subject: Indian Polity
title: Republic Meaning
content: The term 'Republic' in the Preamble indicates that the head of the state (the President) is elected, directly or indirectly, for a fixed term, rather than being a hereditary monarch.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Overview and Location
content: Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, covering Articles 12 to 35. They are often called the 'Magna Carta' of India.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Six Categories
content: There are currently six Fundamental Rights: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Right to Property Removed
content: The Right to Property was originally a Fundamental Right (Article 31) but was removed by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1978. It now exists only as a legal right under Article 300A.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Right to Equality Articles
content: The Right to Equality is covered under Articles 14 to 18, including equality before law, prohibition of discrimination, equality of opportunity in public employment, and abolition of untouchability and titles.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Article 17 - Untouchability
content: Article 17 abolishes 'untouchability' in any form and forbids its practice. Enforcement of any disability arising from untouchability is a punishable offence.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Right to Freedom - Article 19
content: Article 19 guarantees six freedoms to citizens: freedom of speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession/occupation.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Article 21 - Right to Life
content: Article 21 guarantees the Right to Life and Personal Liberty, stating that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Right against Exploitation
content: Articles 23-24 form the Right against Exploitation. Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour. Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines, or hazardous work.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Right to Constitutional Remedies
content: Article 32 gives citizens the right to directly approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Five Writs
content: Under Article 32 and Article 226, courts can issue five types of writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Cultural and Educational Rights
content: Articles 29-30 protect the interests of minorities, giving them the right to conserve their distinct language, script, or culture, and the right to establish and administer educational institutions.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Overview and Location
content: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in Part IV of the Constitution, covering Articles 36 to 51. They were borrowed from the Irish Constitution.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Non-Justiciable Nature
content: Directive Principles are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by any court. However, they are declared to be 'fundamental in the governance of the country'.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Classification
content: DPSPs are broadly classified into three categories: Socialist principles, Gandhian principles, and Liberal-Intellectual principles.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Article 39 - Equal Pay
content: Article 39 directs the State to ensure equal pay for equal work for both men and women, and equitable distribution of material resources for the common good.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Article 40 - Village Panchayats
content: Article 40 directs the State to take steps to organize village panchayats and endow them with powers to function as units of self-government (a Gandhian principle).

subject: Indian Polity
title: Article 44 - Uniform Civil Code
content: Article 44 directs the State to secure for citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Article 45 - Education for Children
content: Article 45 originally directed the State to provide free and compulsory education for children until age 14. This has since been strengthened by the 86th Amendment, which added Article 21A as a Fundamental Right.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Article 48 - Agriculture and Cattle
content: Article 48 directs the State to organize agriculture and animal husbandry on modern scientific lines and to take steps for preserving and improving breeds, prohibiting slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch/draught cattle.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Article 51 - International Peace
content: Article 51 directs the State to promote international peace and security, and to maintain just and honourable relations between nations.

subject: Indian Polity
title: President - Head of State
content: The President of India is the head of state under Article 52, and formally the head of the Executive, though real executive power lies with the Council of Ministers.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Presidential Election
content: The President is elected by an electoral college consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of States (and UTs of Delhi and Puducherry).

subject: Indian Polity
title: Term of President
content: Under Article 56, the President holds office for a term of 5 years from the date on which he/she enters upon the office, and is eligible for re-election.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Vice President Role
content: The Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64) and acts as President when there is a vacancy in that office.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Prime Minister
content: The Prime Minister is the real head of the executive, appointed by the President, usually the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Council of Ministers
content: Under Article 75, the Council of Ministers, headed by the Prime Minister, is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Attorney General
content: Under Article 76, the Attorney General of India is the highest law officer of the country, appointed by the President.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Pardoning Power
content: Article 72 gives the President the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment, including in cases involving death sentences.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Governor - Head of State
content: Under Article 153, there shall be a Governor for each state, who acts as the head of the state executive.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Appointment of Governor
content: The Governor is appointed by the President under Article 155, and holds office during the pleasure of the President (Article 156), usually for a term of 5 years.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Chief Minister
content: The Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor, and is usually the leader of the majority party or coalition in the state Legislative Assembly.

subject: Indian Polity
title: State Council of Ministers
content: The Council of Ministers, headed by the Chief Minister, is collectively responsible to the state Legislative Assembly.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Advocate General
content: Under Article 165, the Advocate General is the chief law officer of a state, appointed by the Governor.

subject: Indian Polity
title: Reserving Bills for President
content: Under Article 200, the Governor may reserve certain bills passed by the state legislature for the consideration of the President.
